Lellinger|access-date=2011-02-20}}}} '''''Niphidium crassifolium''''', commonly known as the '''graceful fern''', is a species of [[fern]] in the family [[Polypodiaceae]] found in Central and South America. It is predominantly [[epiphytic]], growing on other plants—for example, in the canopies of trees—but occasionally [[epipetric|grows on rocks]] or on the ground, particularly at higher altitude. It has a [[rhizome]] from which many fine [[rootlet]]s covered in dark reddish-brown scales grow.{{cite book|author=Thomas B. Croat|title=Flora of Barro Colorado Island|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Whc_ahfhFFoC&pg=PA102|access-date=20 February 2011|year=1978|publisher=Stanford University Press|isbn=978-0-8047-0950-7|pages=102–}} Together they form a root basket that, when growing on trees, helps to trap leaf litter and dust, forming a nutrient-rich soil that holds water.{{cite book|author=Egbert Giles Leigh|author-link1=Egbert Giles Leigh|title=Tropical forest ecology: a view from Barro Colorado Island|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LFHwAAAAMAAJ|access-date=20 February 2011|year=1999|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-509602-6}} Its leaves are simple in shape, {{convert|13|-|85|cm|in|0}} long and {{convert|3|-|5|cm|in}} wide and when dry, and covered by a wax-like film. The [[Sorus|sori]] are round and large, occurring in single rows between veins at the far end of the leaf. ==Taxonomy== [[File:Polypodium crassifolium0.jpg|thumb|left|A closeup of the underside of a frond of ''N. crassifolium'', showing the [[Sorus|sori]]]] ''N. crassifolium'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753 as ''Polypodium crassifolium''. In 1972, [[David B. Lellinger]] moved the species into the genus ''[[Niphidium]]''. It can be difficult to distinguish from ''[[Niphidium albopunctatissimum|N. albopunctatissimum]]'', but that species has narrower leaves and is mostly found growing on rocks or on the ground, as well as occupying a different range.{{cite book|author1=Barbara Joe Hoshizaki|author2=Robbin Craig Moran|title=Fern grower's manual|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wq_-jexfHCcC&pg=PA398|access-date=20 February 2011|year=2001|publisher=Timber Press|isbn=978-0-88192-495-4|pages=398–}} ==Distribution== ''Niphidium crassifolium'' is found in Central and South America, from Mexico in the north to Peru in the south and including Panama, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana and the West Indies. It grows at altitudes up to {{convert|1100|m|ft}} above sea level and over a wide range of humidity.{{cite book|author=Jürgen Nieder|title=Epiphytes and canopy fauna of the Otonga rain forest (Ecuador)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cqRjLPRhi9IC&pg=PA99|access-date=20 February 2011|date=31 August 2001|publisher=BoD – Books on Demand|isbn=978-3-8311-1858-8|pages=99–}} According to Thomas Croat, it is probably the most common fern found on [[Barro Colorado Island]], Panama. ''Niphidium crassifolium'' is known to grow on ''[[Socratea exorrhiza]]'', occurring on 12% of individuals on Barro Colorado Island.{{Cite journal| url = http://si-pddr.si.edu/dspace/bitstream/10088/2257/1/Zotz_and_Vollrath.pdf| year = 2003| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110827065056/http://si-pddr.si.edu/dspace/bitstream/10088/2257/1/Zotz_and_Vollrath.pdf| archive-date = 2011-08-27| doi = 10.1017/S0266467403003092| volume = 19| journal = Journal of Tropical Ecology| first1 = G.| last2 = Vollrath| first2 = B.| title = The epiphyte vegetation of the palm Socratea exorrhiza - correlations with tree size, tree age and bryophyte cover| last1 = Zotz| pages = 81–90| s2cid = 56431960| access-date = 2015-08-29| url-status = live}} It is also known to grow on ''[[Platypodium elegans]]'', ''[[Ceiba pentandra]]'', ''[[Tabebuia guayacan]]'' and ''[[Anacardium excelsum]]''.{{cite journal | doi = 10.1111/j.1744-7429.1997.tb00427.x| author = Jose Luis Andrade and Park S. Nobel | year = 1997 | title = Microhabitats and Water Relations of Epiphytic Cacti and Ferns in a Lowland Neotropical Forest | journal = Biotropica | volume = 29 | issue = 3 | pages = 261–270 | jstor = 2389141 | bibcode = 1997Biotr..29..261A }} ==Biochemistry== This species uses [[crassulacean acid metabolism]] (CAM), whereby it stores some carbon dioxide produced by [[cellular respiration|respiration]] at night and releases this for use in [[photosynthesis]] the next day, but the overall contribution of this is small compared to that of true CAM plants such as cacti. Under drought stress, the contribution of CAM increases from 2.7% of total [[carbon fixation]] to 10%.{{cite book|author1=Klaus Mehltreter|author2=Lawrence R. Walker|author3=Joanne M. Sharpe|title=Fern Ecology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J0L8EdRYmYIC&pg=PA166|access-date=20 February 2011|year=2010|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-72820-1|pages=166–}} The production of [[gametophyte]]s is determined by light levels rather than by a [[plant hormone|hormone]].{{cite book|author=Valayamghat Raghavan|title=Developmental biology of fern gametophytes|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZSS9Al0HHtwC&pg=PA217|access-date=20 February 2011|year=1989|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-33022-0|pages=217–}} ==Uses== ''N. crassifolium'' can be cultivated, growing well in well-drained soil under medium light. It is reported to be able to survive consecutive days of freezing temperatures down to {{convert|-7|C|F}}. In Northern Peru the fresh stem is used in traditional medicine to treat inflammation of internal organs.{{cite journal|url=http://nopr.niscair.res.in/handle/123456789/10330 |title=Antibacterial activity of medicinal plants of Northern Peru – can traditional applications provide leads for modern science? |journal=Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge |volume=9 |issue=4 |date=October 2010 |access-date=2011-02-20|author1-link=Rainer W.
